doc.title: Chico Hamilton — Smithsonian Jazz Oral History

title: Developing a touch and a sound, with a demonstration
summary: He says sound comes from developing a touch, which he teaches students, then plays on the drums to show how cymbals and brushes can swing an orchestra.

story.theme_name: Drummers and drumming: who played what, and how
story.community_name: Great drummers: who they admired and why

blocks.x: How would you describe what it is that is you on the drums?
It’s the way that I play. It’s the sound that I get. That’s the whole bottom line, man, is getting the sound. The only way you can get a sound is by developing a touch.
So is that the same thing as feel, other people say the feel, okay.

Develop a touch. And developing a touch you’ll get a sound, regardless of what instrument you play on, it doesn’t matter. It can be the worse set of drums, tubs in the world, but you get your sound. When you sit down and play they know it’s you. This is what I teach; this is what I stress when, you know, young players come for lessons, things like that, you know. Get your own touch. You know, how many sounds are in a cymbal?
Uh-huh, uh-huh. I’ll show you. You want me -- but we’re talking right now.
We’ll show it tomorrow. I’ll take a microphone over there. You can definitely show it. We’ll do it tomorrow though.
Matter of fact, I’m kind of talked out a little bit.
You want to go and play? Do you have to set up. I mean we can put it on -­
No, I just want to go show you something.

Okay, let’s cool it for a minute huh? (Musical sounds). You can swing a 100­ piece orchestra. (Musical sounds). That’s what you call -- (musical sounds). That’s getting a sound. (Musical sounds).
